newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG caretaker leader vows to punish mutineers.
newsitem.headline: PNG caretaker leader vows to punish mutineers.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's government on Thursday appointed a caretaker prime minister who pledged to restore peace to this troubled South Pacific nation, but said mutinous soldiers should not be spared punishment.
Mining and Petroleum Minister John Giheno was appointed to fill in for Sir Julius Chan, who stood aside in the face of civilian and military protests demanding his resignation.
Giheno, regarded as an outsider in the leadership race, told reporters he would restore peace to the capital but that mutinous soldiers who joined protests should be charged.

"In regard to the soldiers, the mutiny...you break a law, you expect the consequences," Giheno said, minutes before he was sworn in by Governor-General Sir Wiwa Korowi at Government House, a hill-top colonial building overlooking the sea.
But Giheno said the final decision on requests by army leaders for immunity for their men was up to the cabinet.

Chan announced on Wednesday that he, his deputy and Finance Minister Chris Haiveta, and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape would stand aside pending an inquiry into a $36 million contract to use mercenaries to quell an island rebellion.
Chan said the move was aimed at defusing the 10-day political crisis, the worst in this impoverished South Pacific nation's 22 years of independence.

Thousands of protesters gathered outside parliament on Tuesday demanding Chan's resignation and rebel soldiers blockaded parliament throughout Tuesday night, trapping about 100 politicians inside after a parliamentary motion demanding that Chan step aside failed to pass.
Chan has not resigned and Giheno said he could return as prime minister as soon as he was cleared by the inquiry.
"I'm just looking after the job," he said.
After day-long talks interrupted by the final parliamentary sitting before regular national elections in June, the cabinet appointed Forests Minister Andrew Baing as Giheno's deputy.
Commerce Minister Nakikus Konga was given the finance portfolio and Giheno takes on defence.

Giheno said he would seek a meeting with the sacked military chief, Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who sparked the crisis by demanding Chan's resignation over the hiring of mercenaries to fight secessionists on Bougainville island.
Giheno said he would not decide on Singirok's future in the military until the completion of the inquiry, which is to be conducted from April 1 to 18.
Singirok, who remains popular among Papua New Guinea's 4,000-strong armed forces, has asked for immunity from prosecution for rebellious troops.
Giheno appeared to reject calls to widen the inquiry to widespread allegations of political corruption.
"I think cabinet has already made a decision and its position are very, very clear," he said.
After a day of celebrations on Wednesday, the capital of Port Moresby returned to normal on Thursday.
Buses were running and shops, businesses and banks were open. Outside parliament house, street cleaners picked up the debris of the protests against Chan.

Papua New Guinea-linked stocks listed in Australia jumped in early trade on Thursday, and analysts said investors were relieved not just that stability had returned, but that PNG's democratic institutions had survived.
"Everyone is relieved that the parliamentary process actually worked and that we didn't go into a period of military control," said David Walker of ABN AMRO bank.
